analysis.one_liner: Ends the unelected federal board overseeing Puerto Rico's finances once the island sets up its own replacement.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on March 5, 2026 and referred to two House committees; no committee or floor action has been taken since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the 2016 law (PROMESA) that put an unelected federal Oversight Board in charge of Puerto Rico's finances and bankruptcy cases. Under it, the Board would automatically shut down the day after Puerto Rico's own government passes legislation creating a replacement entity, and that new entity — or the Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority — would take over representing Puerto Rico in future debt-restructuring cases. Existing fiscal plans, court oversight, and bankruptcy confirmation rules would stay in place.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, Puerto Rico's elected government and its residents would regain direct control over the island's fiscal policy and debt restructuring, ending the Oversight Board's authority to approve budgets and represent Puerto Rico in bankruptcy. The Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority or a successor entity would represent the island in future debt cases instead of the Board.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Puerto Rico's residents and elected government

how_it_helps.text: It adds a termination mechanism to PROMESA: the unelected Oversight Board would automatically dissolve the day after Puerto Rico enacts legislation creating a successor entity.

It transfers control of future Puerto Rico debt-restructuring cases from the Oversight Board to the Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority or a successor entity chosen by Puerto Rico's own government, while keeping existing certified budgets, prior plans, and federal court jurisdiction unchanged.

analysis.who_pays: Creditors and bondholders who relied on the Board's oversight would face a locally chosen debtor representative in future cases. Anyone relying on the Board's continued fiscal oversight loses that backstop, though certified budgets and court jurisdiction are preserved.
analysis.who_pays_short: Creditors relying on the Board's oversight

drawbacks.text: The bill lets the Puerto Rico legislature create a successor entity that would take over the Oversight Board's role as debtor representative in bankruptcy cases, and would retain the Board's professional staff unless the new legislation says otherwise — a mechanism that depends entirely on the Commonwealth choosing a credible successor.

The bill preserves fiscal plans and budgets the Board already certified and leaves bankruptcy court jurisdiction unchanged, so it would not undo decisions made under Board oversight — some Puerto Rico residents criticized the Board's austerity budgets even as the bill leaves those plans standing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If enacted, the bill would end what critics call an unelected governing body over Puerto Rico, while preserving court oversight and existing certified budgets. The main risk is that a Commonwealth-designated successor could reopen settled fiscal decisions; the bill tries to limit that by keeping prior fiscal plans and court jurisdiction intact. As introduced with no committee action, neither the benefit nor the cost has been tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the House and sent to two committees, and no committee has taken it up since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 5, 2026 and referred to the House Natural Resources and Judiciary Committees.
No further action — no hearings, markups, or floor votes — appears in the record since the referral.
It has only one cosponsor in the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained or lost yet; the Oversight Board remains in place because the bill has not moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Oversight Board, which remains in place

for.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and have taken no recorded action on it since.

sides.party_line_note: Only two House Democrats are attached to the bill and no votes have occurred, so no party split is visible in the record.

industries.industry: Bondholders and creditors of Puerto Rico and its public utilities
industries.note: A locally chosen successor could steer future debt restructurings away from the Board's creditor-friendly approach, affecting recoveries in future cases. Prior fiscal plans and certified budgets are preserved, limiting the change.

industries.industry: Bankruptcy and financial advisory professionals serving PROMESA cases
industries.note: The bill requires that the Oversight Board's professionals, advisors, and counsel be retained by any successor entity, keeping the same expert infrastructure in place after the transition.

industries.industry: Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority and its ratepayers
industries.note: PREPA or its successor would represent Puerto Rico in future debt cases, giving the island's government direct control over how its power authority's debt is handled — an outcome ratepayers could benefit from through lower debt burdens, depending on how the successor is structured.

analysis.trajectory: With one cosponsor, no hearings or markups, and dual referral to two committees, the bill is highly unlikely to advance in the 119th Congress; most private-member bills at this stage never receive committee action.
